name: 六级模拟卷 · 第一套

writing.prompt:
Part I Writing (30 minutes)

Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay that begins with the sentence "In an age of endless notifications, the ability to focus has become a superpower." You can make comments, cite examples or use your personal experiences to develop the essay. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.ideas: 审题思路:引句已锁定主题——注意力稀缺时代的专注力。推荐三段式:① 首段承接引句,指出分心环境的普遍性与代价;② 中间段论证专注为何是超能力(深度工作的产出、学习效果),可举学习/工作对比例;③ 结尾给出获得专注的可操作做法并升华。
writing.model:
In an age of endless notifications, the ability to focus has become a superpower. While our devices compete fiercely for every spare second of attention, those who can concentrate on one task for hours accomplish what others merely plan to do.
The reason is simple: meaningful work demands depth. A student who checks social media every few minutes may spend five hours at a desk yet retain less than a classmate who studies with the phone in another room for ninety minutes. Research on task switching confirms that every interruption leaves a residue, and shallow attention produces shallow results, whether in reading, writing or coding.
Fortunately, focus can be trained like a muscle. We can schedule blocks of deep work, silence non-essential notifications and treat boredom in queues as a chance to think rather than a gap to fill with scrolling.
Concentration, in short, is not a personality trait but a daily choice. Whoever chooses it deliberately will hold a quiet advantage in a distracted world.
writing.notes: 亮点表达:spare second(碎片时间)/leave a residue(留下残留成本)/trained like a muscle(像肌肉一样训练)/hold a quiet advantage(保有隐性优势)。结构:现象-论证-方法-升华,论证段用对比例证,是六级高分常用套路。

listening.intro: Questions 1 to 4 are based on the conversation you have just heard. 先听第一遍做题,再逐句精听对照。
listening.questions:
1. What happened to Daniel's internship applications?
A) He received several offers from big companies.
B) Most companies turned him down for lack of experience.
C) He withdrew his applications halfway.
D) His professor refused to write a recommendation.

2. How does the woman view Daniel's part-time bookstore job?
A) It is irrelevant to his career goals.
B) It taught him customer service and responsibility.
C) It should be removed from the resume.
D) It proves he is unfit for office work.

3. What does the woman suggest adding to the resume?
A) Personal hobbies and photos.
B) A list of courses and grades.
C) Action verbs and concrete numbers.
D) Praise from former classmates.

4. What is the woman's attitude towards rejection?
A) It signals the applicant should change careers.
B) It rarely happens to well-prepared students.
C) It is a normal part of the process.
D) It means the resume was badly written.
listening.analysis:
1. 细节题。对话开头 Daniel 自述"only two replied, and both turned me down for lack of experience",对应 B。A/C/D 均与原文矛盾或未提及。
2. 细节题。女士说书店兼职教会他 customer service and responsibility,即 B 中的可迁移能力。
3. 细节题。女士建议 highlight transferable skills,并且 add numbers,action verbs 开头,对应 C。
4. 观点题。女士结尾说 rejection is part of the process,正确答案 C。A/B/D 均属过度推断。

listening.intro: Questions 5 to 7 are based on the passage you have just heard.
listening.questions:
5. What do psychologists say procrastination really is?
A) A problem of emotion management.
B) A problem of poor timekeeping.
C) A sign of low intelligence.
D) A habit that cannot be changed.

6. Why did the ten-minute group perform better in the experiment?
A) They were given more time in total.
B) They cared more about their grades.
C) Starting turned out to be the hardest part.
D) Their report topic was easier.

7. What did the study on self-forgiveness find?
A) Forgiving oneself increases future delays.
B) Harsh self-criticism improves motivation.
C) Forgiving oneself reduces later procrastination.
D) Guilt has no effect on study habits.
listening.analysis:
5. 主旨细节题。开篇即点明 procrastination is a problem of emotion management rather than time management,选 A。
6. 推理题。短文解释实验结果时说 starting is usually the hardest part,一旦开始多数人会继续下去,对应 C。
7. 细节题。原文:students who forgave themselves ... procrastinated less before the next one,选 C。B 与原文相反(harsh self-criticism 推向逃避)。

listening.intro: Questions 8 to 11 are based on the recording you have just heard.
listening.questions:
8. According to the speaker, where do microplastics come from?
A) Only from factories near the ocean.
B) From tiny manufactured beads and fragments of larger plastic.
C) From volcanic ash and desert dust.
D) From chemical fertilizers on farms.

9. Which of the following is mentioned as a place where microplastics have been found?
A) The deepest ocean trenches and highest mountains.
B) Only in coastal cities.
C) In Antarctic ice cores only.
D) In outer space.

10. Why are microplastics extremely difficult to clean up?
A) They sink too deep to reach.
B) They drift through nets designed for larger waste.
C) They dissolve into the water instantly.
D) Cleanup is forbidden by international law.

11. What assignment does the speaker give the students?
A) To design a new kind of washing machine.
B) To calculate which single change would cut the most plastic waste.
C) To interview fishermen in their hometown.
D) To write an essay on ocean currents.
listening.analysis:
8. 细节题。讲座开头明确两个来源:manufactured tiny(如磨砂珠)与 fragments that break off,对应 B。
9. 细节题。原文列举 deepest ocean trenches and the highest mountains,以及盐/水/空气,选 A。
10. 细节题。原文 A net that catches plastic bottles lets the particles drift straight through,即 B。
11. 细节题。结尾布置作业:track your own plastic use for one week and calculate which single change would cut the most waste,对应 B。

reading.title: Section D 仔细阅读
reading.passage:
Digital minimalism, the practice of drastically reducing time spent on screens, started as a fringe movement of overworked programmers. Today it is spreading to campuses and offices around the world, and its advocates include not only exhausted teenagers but also the very engineers who built the apps everyone finds hard to quit.
The logic behind the movement is straightforward. Attention is a limited resource, and every app is designed to consume as much of it as possible. The average smartphone user now touches the device nearly three thousand times a day, and each touch carries a small cognitive cost. Multiplied across a day, these micro-interruptions add up to hours of fragmented thinking, which is why so many people feel busy yet unproductive.
Critics argue that digital minimalism is a luxury of the privileged, who can afford to log off because their jobs do not depend on instant replies. There is some truth here: a delivery rider cannot silence his phone. Yet defenders reply that the movement is not about abandoning technology but about using it deliberately, keeping the tools that serve your goals and dropping those that merely harvest your attention.
Early evidence suggests the benefits are real. In one study, undergraduates who limited social media to thirty minutes a day reported significantly lower loneliness and depression after just three weeks. Companies that introduced no-meeting mornings saw measurable gains in output. None of this requires living like a hermit; it requires deciding, in advance, what technology is for. In a world engineered to distract, that decision may be the most valuable skill of all.
reading.questions:
12. Why do the app engineers mentioned in Paragraph 1 matter?
A) They earn more than ordinary users.
B) Even they struggle to quit the apps they built.
C) They have all joined the movement publicly.
D) They design better minimalism software.

13. According to Paragraph 2, what is the cost of frequent phone touches?
A) Battery drain and extra fees.
B) Hours of fragmented thinking.
C) Damaged eyesight.
D) Weakened social bonds.

14. What criticism do opponents make of digital minimalism?
A) It is too expensive to practice.
B) It harms personal relationships.
C) It is a privilege not everyone can afford.
D) It reduces workplace efficiency.

15. What happened in the undergraduate study?
A) Students quit social media completely.
B) Loneliness and depression dropped within three weeks.
C) Academic performance doubled.
D) Students deleted all their apps.

16. What does the passage suggest as the core of digital minimalism?
A) Living like a hermit.
B) Buying premium tools.
C) Deciding in advance what technology is for.
D) Banning smartphones on campus.
reading.analysis:
12. 细节题。首段 its advocates include the very engineers who built the apps everyone finds hard to quit——连设计者都难以戒断,选 B。
13. 细节题。第二段结尾 micro-interruptions add up to hours of fragmented thinking,选 B。A/C/D 未提及。
14. 观点题。第三段 Critics argue ... a luxury of the privileged,对应 C(外卖骑手的例子即支撑此点)。
15. 细节题。末段实验:limited to thirty minutes a day 后 loneliness and depression 显著下降,选 B。注意 A 的 completely quit 与 thirty minutes 矛盾。
16. 主旨题。结尾 deciding, in advance, what technology is for,选 C。A 与原文 None of this requires living like a hermit 矛盾。

translation.prompt:
Part IV Translation (30 minutes)

Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to translate a passage from Chinese into English.

剪纸是中国最受欢迎的民间艺术之一,已有一千五百多年的历史。艺人们用剪刀或刻刀,把普通的红纸变成花卉、动物和人物等生动图案。每逢节日,人们把这些被称为“窗花”的作品贴在窗户上,表达对未来的美好祝愿。2009年,中国剪纸被列入联合国教科文组织人类非物质文化遗产代表作名录。如今,这门艺术走进了学校课堂和国际展览,向世界传播着中国文化。
translation.reference: Paper cutting is one of the most popular folk arts in China, with a history of more than one thousand five hundred years. Using scissors or carving knives, artisans turn ordinary red paper into vivid patterns of flowers, animals and figures. During festivals, people paste these works, known as window flowers, on their windows to express good wishes for the future. In 2009, Chinese paper cutting was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity of UNESCO. Today, the art has entered school classrooms and international exhibitions, spreading Chinese culture to the world.
translation.notes: 要点解析:① "有着……历史"用 with a history of 结构避免另起短句;② "把……变成"处理为 turn ... into,前用现在分词 Using... 作状语,是六级翻译高频句式;③ "被称为窗花"用过去分词插入语 known as window flowers;④ "被列入……名录"固定译法 be inscribed on the List;⑤ 联合国教科文组织 = UNESCO,机构名先全称后可缩写;⑥ 结尾 spreading... 现在分词作结果状语,衔接自然。
